pitch.short: I spent two years recruiting for Pinewick Paper & Print and three more as the HR business partner for the same three sites. I start with the exit notes, then go and ask the people who wrote them.
why_hire: Nearly six years inside one company, from front desk cover to recruiter to HRBP, so I have watched the same people go from offer letter to exit interview.

about.intro: I grew up in Larchmont Falls and studied psychology and sociology at Ashgrove College. In autumn 2019 I covered Tilly Brandt's lunch breaks on the front desk at Pinewick Paper & Print, which is where I learned who actually runs the office. By October I was HR coordinator, and in 2020 Priya Raman made me the company's first in-house recruiter. In 2021 I ran the autumn rush hiring. In 2022 I became HR business partner to about 260 people across three sites, working on orientation, early exits and job grades. In 2025 I started an MBA at Harrowgate School of Management to move into broader people strategy.
about.now: Writing The Third Drawer, a monthly newsletter on the HR paperwork nobody reads, running a crossword club, and rehearsing for a folk-dance evening at Falls Hall in January.

new-hire-orientation.context: Pinewick's three sites took on about 40 new starters a quarter in 2022, across the warehouse, the print works and the sales office. Orientation was Gordie Pruitt's three-hour welcome talk, ending with a whiteboard acronym, then lunch, then each team did its own thing.
new-hire-orientation.problem: Of 138 new starters in 2022, 18.8% were gone inside 90 days. The exit notes repeated the same things: nobody said what good looked like, and badges and logins took days to arrive. Every early departure took a supervisor roughly three weeks of re-hiring and retraining.
what_i_did: Went through 31 exit-interview notes and phoned 12 of the people who quit during their first 90 days.
Mapped the first 90 days with five recent joiners and their supervisors: 36 steps across seven owners, none tracked after week one.
Rebuilt orientation around five checkpoints: badge and login ready before day one, a named floor buddy, a first solo task in week two, a pulse and chat at day 30, and goals on paper by day 60.
Ran 30-minute sessions for 26 supervisors and team leads, each leaving with a single-sheet guide to the conversations at days 7, 30, 60 and 90.
Built pulse forms for days 30 and 60 plus a cohort retention view in Looker Studio, which the site managers reviewed monthly.

decisions.choice: Start with weeks one and two, not the 90-day plan
decisions.why: Most early leavers I phoned said they had already decided in week three, which made the opening checkpoints the ones that counted.

decisions.choice: Buddies chosen by supervisors, at most two joiners each
decisions.why: Buddies given three or more joiners had drifted away within a month.

decisions.choice: Track each joining cohort instead of each quarter
decisions.why: Quarterly figures were tiny and moved with hiring volume, while a cohort let us follow one group through the same weeks.

results.note: 164 hires, Q2 2023 – Q1 2024, vs 138 hires in 2022

new-hire-orientation.learned: On day zero, a working badge and login beat every training session. Joiners who waited two days or more for their access were nearly twice as likely to leave within 90 days. The fix was a desk-prep checklist, started at offer acceptance and run by Tilly Brandt, who had been doing it informally for years.
new-hire-orientation.next: Extend the same checkpoints to staff who transfer between sites, who had no orientation at all.
new-hire-orientation.my_role: HR Business Partner; owned the redesign and the tracking
new-hire-orientation.dates: March to August 2023, followed through to March 2024

depot-first-month.context: Tallow Bay Freight runs eight regional depots. Its four busiest took on about 30 new dock hands a month between them, many in their first warehouse job.
depot-first-month.problem: 21% of new dock hands left within three weeks, mostly in the second week. Each exit meant a short-handed shift and another round of interviews for the depot supervisor.
what_i_did: Held 46 conversations with dock hands, on break and at the tea urn, and made 15 exit calls.
Shadowed five early and four late shifts and read three months of depot incident and HR tickets.
Set up a boot-fit station for day one, so every new hand left the stores with safety boots that fit instead of the nearest size.
Designed a pocket-sized bay card for supervisors: today's bay, who to ask, and any change to tomorrow's bay, handed over before the end of the shift.
Ran the pilot in four depots against four matched control depots for five weeks.

decisions.choice: A boot-fit station, not a safety talk
decisions.why: Hands told me sore feet in week one was why they stopped coming. A fitting took ten minutes and stores staff could do it.
Supervisors wore gloves and had no spare hands. A card in a shirt pocket would get used; an app would not.
Hiring and exits swing with peak shipping weeks, so comparing before with after would have fooled us.

results.note: pilot depots; control depots went from 20% to 19%

depot-first-month.learned: Small physical comforts decided more exits than any engagement idea. Hands moved to another bay without warning in week two often left by week three, so telling them the night before mattered as much as the boots.
depot-first-month.next: Roll the boot-fit station out to all eight depots, add the bay card to the day-one welcome pack, and measure six-week attrition over a full quarter.
depot-first-month.my_role: People Operations Intern, working with the depot HR lead and regional ops

staff-survey-readout.context: Ferncliff Biscuit Works, a 380-person maker in Wexley Heights, held its first staff survey in autumn 2025. The people manager was holding 281 responses and a 36-page export, and wanted our team to produce a plan from them.
staff-survey-readout.problem: Company-wide eNPS was +9, which looked healthy, but it hid wide gaps between teams. Team heads could not tell which of the 36 questions deserved action.
what_i_did: Cleaned the Typeform export and grouped 36 questions into six drivers.
Drew a team-by-driver heat map that only displays a team once seven or more of its people had replied.
Used Python for a driver analysis, to find which drivers tracked eNPS most closely.
Held six focus groups with 34 staff in the canteen, with no supervisors in the room and the ovens switched off.
Led a 90-minute workshop in which eight team heads settled on three actions, then sent a pulse survey six weeks later.

decisions.why: With a single people manager on staff, only a short list of changes with named owners would actually get done.

decisions.choice: No team results under seven responses
decisions.why: On a small team a supervisor could have guessed every author, and response rates the following year would have slumped.

results.note: packing hall and dispatch, out of 5

staff-survey-readout.learned: The focus groups explained the numbers. Packing-hall staff scored suggestions low because the suggestion box was emptied once a quarter and nobody was told what happened next. Emptying it weekly and posting replies on the canteen board did more than a supervisor workshop would have.
staff-survey-readout.next: Repeat the pulse each quarter, and hold stay interviews with line supervisors, whose teams were starting to lose people.

autumn-rush-hiring.context: Pinewick's busiest months run from late August to early December, when school orders and holiday cards arrive together. In 2021 the warehouse and the sales counters needed 60 extra people, and the usual method was a phone screen and a handshake from Gordie.
autumn-rush-hiring.problem: Earlier rush seasons lost about a third of seasonal hires within a fortnight, and Marla Finch's sales desk and the warehouse each claimed the strongest candidates, which left the rest to whoever shouted loudest.
what_i_did: Posted the roles on local job boards, at two colleges and through a staff referral scheme with a coffee-voucher reward, which Dennis Hale approved after rounding it to whole dollars.
Replaced the phone screen with a twenty-minute parcel-packing trial at the Larchmont Falls warehouse, set up with Wendell Odom.
Tracked every candidate in one shared sheet and ran a fair split of the strongest candidates between the sales desks and the warehouse each Friday.
Sent each of the 72 offer holders a short check-in the week before their start date.

decisions.choice: A work trial instead of a phone screen
decisions.why: Wendell wanted to see how people handled a tape gun and a tight deadline, which is most of the job.

decisions.choice: A fair weekly split of the strongest candidates
decisions.why: Without it the sales desks and the warehouse competed for the same people, and Marla's desk would have won every week.

autumn-rush-hiring.learned: The days between the offer and the first shift needed as much care as selection. Years later, as HRBP, I found myself supporting many of the people I had hired that autumn.

job-grades-pay-bands.context: Pinewick had grown by taking over two small print shops, and titles had been handed out site by site, once or twice by Gordie on the spot. The list included a 'Paper Evangelist', a title he had created for himself.
job-grades-pay-bands.problem: Across the company there were 44 titles, and pay for one title could vary by 35%. A promotion at one site meant something different at the next, and nobody could explain how.
what_i_did: Sat down with Dennis Hale, who already had every title in a spreadsheet with one tab per site, and listed all 44 along with who held them.
Wrote a six-grade specialist track and a three-grade lead track with the three site managers, grade by grade.
Mapped all of the roughly 260 staff to the new grades.
Used regional market data to set a pay band for each grade and marked every person falling outside theirs.

decisions.choice: Two tracks: six specialist grades and three lead grades
decisions.why: A skilled printer or picker had to be able to progress without taking on a team.

decisions.choice: Bands from market data, not current pay
decisions.why: Pay already varied by 35% within a single title, and bands based on it would have preserved that spread. Dennis asked for bands rounded to the nearest $250 and, for once, nobody argued.

job-grades-pay-bands.learned: The site managers had to write the grade descriptions with us. A manager who had written a grade could explain it to their own team; a grade handed down from HR could not be.
job-grades-pay-bands.my_role: HR Business Partner, co-author with the finance team and three site managers

plain-english-handbook.context: Small employers around Wexley Heights kept their staff rules in long handbooks copied from larger firms.
plain-english-handbook.problem: New starters did not read them, and the office manager or owner fielded the same questions about leave, sick pay and overtime every week.
what_i_did: Wrote twelve one-page policies in plain English, each with the rule, an example and who to ask.
Added a five-question check to each policy, so new starters can see what they have understood.
Rolled it out at three small employers and revised it each month after hearing from them.

decisions.why: A single page can be pinned in the canteen and read in the time it takes the kettle to boil.
Asking questions showed which wording confused people, which I could not see from the rules alone. It also came from the orientation pulses I had run at Pinewick.

results.metric: Repeat questions to the office manager

plain-english-handbook.learned: A kit gets used when it suits how a small firm already runs. Listening to users each month paid off more than writing extra policies.
plain-english-handbook.my_role: Built it alone, with three small employers as users
plain-english-handbook.dates: 2025–26, built in six weeks and then adjusted monthly

case-challenge.context: Term 3 People Strategy Challenge at Harrowgate School of Management: a 1,200-person printing group had proposed a four-day week for every site, and each team had two days to advise the board.
case-challenge.problem: Moving every team to four days together threatened gaps in service and annoyed customers, and the case said nothing about which teams could manage it.
what_i_did: Guided a team of four through the two days.
Sent a short questionnaire around our professional network and collected 52 answers within 30 hours.
Used the answers to rate cover risk for each team.
Recommended a staggered trial, reviewed at six months, and built the slides in Canva.

decisions.choice: Gather our own evidence before anything else
decisions.why: The case was silent on how staff felt, and an estimate resting on 52 real answers was simpler to defend.

decisions.choice: A team-by-team trial with a six-month review
decisions.why: Teams needed different levels of cover, so a single rule for 1,200 people was a poor fit, and the review gave the group a way to change course.

case-challenge.learned: Even with two days, a little real evidence made the advice stronger than a framework by itself.

third-drawer.context: The Third Drawer is a LinkedIn newsletter, published monthly since 2024, on the forms, policies and notices employees skip. The name comes from the drawer at Pinewick where all of them went.
third-drawer.problem: Most writing about HR documents is for lawyers or for HR teams. The people the paperwork is meant for, from warehouse hands to new starters, rarely get a version they can use.
what_i_did: Published an issue each month from 2024 on, every one based on something I had seen at work.
Altered the names and figures in every story so nobody can be recognised from it.
Designed every cover in Canva, including those for 'The form with fourteen signatures' and 'What a fire-drill notice taught me about policy'.

decisions.why: Readers can test a single genuine pattern against their own workplace.
The stories come from real people's situations, and they should not be recognisable.

third-drawer.learned: Writing every month made me write down what each project had taught me while it was still fresh.

values: Read the exit notes before proposing anything.
Never report a team's survey results when fewer than seven people answered.
Give supervisors one small task a week, and check it got done, preferably over tea.
